title: Artificial nests give Hong Kong’s cockatoos a home – and a chance to study their behavior
summary: In busy Hong Kong, conservationists are climbing city trees to install cozy nest boxes for the critically endangered yellow-crested cockatoo. The city's feral flock, now the largest wild population outside Indonesia and Timor-Leste, is giving researchers a rare chance to study the birds' behavior while helping them breed safely. Genetic tests even show these urban cockatoos carry surprisingly rich diversity, a hopeful sign for the species' future.

alt: A white cockatoo with a yellow crest perches happily beside a wooden nest box on a leafy city tree, with Hong Kong's hazy skyline in the distance.

title: Probiotics prevented coral bleaching during a Red Sea heat wave: Study
summary: Scientists gave a patch of Red Sea coral a dose of beneficial bacteria, and when a scorching heat wave hit in 2022, those treated corals stayed vividly healthy while others around them bleached. It's the first real-world proof that coral probiotics can help reefs survive marine heat waves, offering a hopeful new tool as oceans keep warming.

title: Wildlife traffickers are now targeting Indonesia’s critically endangered maleo birds
summary: Maleo birds, found only on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, bury their eggs in warm volcanic sand instead of sitting on nests, which makes both the birds and their eggs easy targets. Reports now show wildlife traffickers turning their attention to this already critically endangered species, adding a new danger on top of habitat loss. Conservationists are worried this growing illegal trade could push the rare bird even closer to disappearing.
caption: Keeping watch over eggs in the sand
alt: A worried-looking maleo bird with a helmet-shaped head stands over a disturbed sandy nest mound on a dusky volcanic beach in Sulawesi, with faint footprints trailing away and a calm teal sea behind it.

title: Dolphins keep their social and hunting lives in separate waters, study finds
summary: A new study finds that dolphins tend to use their social whistles in one set of waters and switch to quick echolocation clicks when hunting prey in another. Researchers say this separation suggests dolphins organize their daily lives much like we divide work from play, keeping chatty reunions and focused hunts in different parts of their home range. The findings offer a sweet new window into how clever and social these ocean mammals really are.

title: Reintroduced Grauer’s gorilla gives birth in DRC national park, ‘makes us happy’
summary: Lulingu, a Grauer's gorilla once rescued from traffickers and raised at the GRACE sanctuary, was released into Virunga National Park in 2024 and has now given birth to a healthy baby. Caretakers are thrilled, since every birth matters for this critically endangered ape, and the community will soon vote on a name for the newborn. The park still faces conflict and poaching pressures, but this birth is a rare bright spot.

title: In war-torn South Sudan, giraffes retain a surprisingly healthy gene pool
summary: Despite decades of war in South Sudan, researchers found that the tiny surviving population of Nubian giraffes is surprisingly genetically diverse and only lightly inbred. Scientists say gene flow across the White Nile has helped keep the population healthy, offering hope that conflict-affected landscapes can still safeguard wildlife. Conservationists now see South Sudan as an unexpected stronghold for this critically endangered giraffe subspecies.

summary: In South Africa, Shannon Hoffman runs a breeding program racing to save the critically endangered African bearded vulture.
